Mercury. A heavy, silvery transition metal and the only metal that remains liquid at room temperature. Known historically as quicksilver, it's highly toxic and bioaccumulates through aquatic food webs as methylmercury, causing neurological damage in a condition called Minamata disease. Despite its toxicity, mercury's unique liquid state, high density, and electrical conductivity made it indispensable in thermometers, barometers, electrical switches, and fluorescent lamps.

Mercury is extracted chiefly from cinnabar, a bright-red mineral of mercury sulfide that is roasted to release mercury vapour. Mercury forms liquid or solid alloys called amalgams with most metals—gold, silver, sodium—but does not amalgamate with iron, so liquid mercury can safely be stored in iron flasks. Evangelista Torricelli used mercury as the fluid for the first barometer in sixteen forty-three, leading to the pressure unit millimeters of mercury, or Torr. In nineteen eleven, Heike Kamerlingh Onnes cooled mercury to four point two Kelvin and discovered superconductivity when its electrical resistance dropped to zero. Mercury forms the calomel electrode, a reference electrode in electrochemistry made from mercury and mercury chloride dissolved in potassium chloride solution. Gold readily dissolves in mercury to form amalgams, historically used in gold extraction. Oxygen played a crucial role when Joseph Priestley heated mercuric oxide and discovered oxygen gas. Sodium combines with mercury to form sodium amalgam, a widely used reducing agent in organic synthesis.
